A crested, toothed fishing pterosaur from Brazil's Santana Formation, known from beautifully preserved three-dimensional skulls that reveal the shape of its bony head crest.
A Brazilian pterosaur carrying a tall sail-like crest on a short, parrot-beaked skull.
The African elephant, and the reason the Afrotropical realm still has an intact large-mammal fauna when every other realm lost one.
The giraffe, browsing acacia crowns five metres up.
The chimpanzee, our closest living relative, a tool-maker of forest and forest edge.
Africa keeps the intact big-mammal community - elephants, rhinos, hippos - that other continents lost.
A fungus farmed in gardens inside termite mounds -- an agriculture tens of millions of years older than our own.
The baobab, storing water in a massively swollen trunk -- the signature tree of seasonally arid Africa.
The flat-topped thorn trees of African savanna, whose spread tracks the Miocene expansion of grassland.
Giant groundsels, tree-sized daisies of the East African summits, each mountain with its own species.
The lion, the only truly social big cat.
Associated with the earliest widely accepted stone tool industries, right at the interval's close.
A heavily-built, small-brained hominin of eastern Africa with huge grinding molars, sharing the early Pleistocene with the first members of Homo.
The quiver tree: a giant tree-aloe of the Namib edge, now dying back at the hot end of its range.
Small-brained, upright-walking hominins; the Laetoli trackway in Tanzania records them walking through volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago.
A moose-shaped giraffid with two pairs of horn-like ossicones, among the heaviest ruminants known.
The gemsbok, tolerating body temperatures that would kill most mammals.
The Atlas cedar, forming the high forests of Morocco and Algeria.
Lucy's species: bipedal, small-brained, and the maker of the Laetoli footprint trail.
The Nile perch, a two-metre predator of the Nile, Chad and Congo systems.
A two-leaved gymnosperm that lives a thousand years on fog alone.
Sugarbushes: the emblem of the Cape fynbos, a fire-dependent heathland with more plant species than any rainforest of its size.
A proboscidean with downward-curving lower tusks, unrelated to any surviving elephant lineage.
A woodland hominin from Ethiopia that walked upright on the ground yet kept a grasping big toe for the trees.
Grasses using the C4 photosynthetic pathway, which is efficient in warm, dry, low-CO2 air. They build tropical savanna from about 8 Ma.
Heavily armoured Tanganyikan snails that look marine, shaped by an arms race with shell-crushing crabs.
African lungfish, surviving the dry season encased in mud.
A late-Miocene Chadian hominin near the split of the human and chimpanzee lines.
Hippos: the closest living relatives of whales. Out of Africa in the late Miocene as far as Britain and Java; dwarf species lived on Madagascar and the Mediterranean islands.
A three-toed grazing horse whose rapid spread across the Old World is a datable event in its own right.
A large Miocene ape from the Siwaliks, close to the ancestry of the orangutan.
An early African ape without a tail, near the base of the hominoid radiation.
taxa.hb: arboreal quadruped

taxa.note: Swamp palms bearing the longest leaves of any plant, along the flooded interior.
Old World monkeys -- baboons, macaques, colobines. African until the late Miocene, then across Eurasia to Japan.
Aardvarks: solitary termite-eaters with peg teeth, the only survivors of their order.
Mastodons: browsing proboscideans with cone-cusped teeth, a separate line from elephants and mammoths. The American mastodon lasted to the end of the Ice Age.
Four-tusked, long-jawed elephant relatives that walked out of Africa at about 19 Ma and eventually reached Patagonia.
Mangrove is the one forest that shows up as coastline rather than as interior vegetation, and it is a Cenozoic feature.
taxa.hb: intertidal tree on stilt roots, salt-excluding

taxa.note: Swamp-dwelling, pig-like artiodactyls of the Old World -- the stock from which hippos arose.
A rhino-like herbivore with two enormous horns, endemic to the Fayum swamps.
A Fayum catarrhine near the base of the Old World monkey and ape split.
An early Fayum proboscidean 2.5 m tall with short tusks in both jaws and the beginnings of a trunk.
A pig-sized, semi-aquatic early proboscidean - a distant, low-slung ancestor of elephants.
Fruit-eating birds -- hornbills, toucans, pigeons. Tropical trees largely depend on them to move seeds, so the forest needs them to regenerate.
Flowering trees closing a canopy overhead. That structure is what makes a rainforest a rainforest, and it does not exist before the Late Cretaceous.
Plants growing on other plants: orchids, bromeliads, ferns. They need a canopy to live in, so they date it.
Woody climbers using trees as scaffolding to reach the light. Like epiphytes, they exist only where there is a canopy.
Grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and large brains -- a group built by and largely confined to closed forest canopy.
An eighteen-metre fully aquatic archaeocete with vestigial hind limbs, preserved by the hundred at Wadi Al-Hitan.
taxa.hb: fully aquatic, serpentine, with vestigial hindlimbs

taxa.note: Horse relatives with claws instead of hooves, knuckle-walking like gorillas and pulling branches down to browse.
Land-living crocodile relatives of the southern continents: long-legged runners, some with mammal-like teeth, some plant-eaters.
Brackish-water snails that radiated into dozens of endemic Lake Pannon species.
Oribatid mites, the slow armoured grazers of leaf litter and moss, in the soil of every land ecosystem since the Devonian.
Springtails, among the first land animals -- Rhyniella from the Rhynie chert is Early Devonian -- and among the last to give up before the ice; they live in every soil on Earth.
Shearing-toothed Mesozoic mammals, the carnivores of their world -- including the one found with a dinosaur inside it.
A colossal titanosaur from the mangrove coasts of Late Cretaceous Egypt (Bahariya).
A titanosaur from the East African rift sediments, part of a distinct southern fauna.
A sail-backed, semi-aquatic theropod larger than T. rex, from the Kem Kem rivers of the Sahara.
A shark-toothed giant predator of the mid-Cretaceous North African floodplains.
A sail-backed, paddle-tailed theropod that hunted fish in North African river systems.
A sauropod with a vacuum-cleaner mouth: five hundred teeth along the square front edge of a featherweight skull, cropping plants at ground level.
A sail-backed iguanodont sharing the lush Cretaceous river deltas of what is now the desert.
An eleven-metre spinosaur of the Sahara's Cretaceous rivers, with a long, narrow, fish-trap snout.
'SuperCroc': a twelve-metre, eight-tonne crocodile relative of the Cretaceous rivers of the Sahara and Brazil.
A hybodont shark with a spine before each dorsal fin and two kinds of teeth, for fish and for shellfish; the commonest shark of Mesozoic seas and rivers.
A towering sauropod from Tanzania's Tendaguru beds, long described as an African species of Brachiosaurus before differences in its skull and proportions placed it in its own genus.
The therapsids with a secondary palate, differentiated teeth and probably fur: the line that produces mammals in the Late Triassic.
A horned, blade-toothed predator that shared the Morrison plain with the larger Allosaurus.
Tendaguru's stegosaur: plates over the shoulders giving way to long paired spikes down the back and tail.
Red deer and their relatives, the characteristic large browsers of the Palearctic woodland and steppe.
Orangutans, the red apes of Borneo and Sumatra, once found north to China.
The nerpa, the world's only wholly freshwater seal, two thousand kilometres from the nearest sea.
The Komodo dragon, a three-metre monitor that evolved in Australia and survives on a few Indonesian islands.
Edelweiss, felted white against ultraviolet light on Alpine limestone.
The largest ape that ever lived, a three-metre orangutan relative known almost entirely from teeth found in Chinese caves and apothecary shops.
The 'Siberian unicorn': a four-tonne steppe rhinoceros with a single enormous horn, which survived until about 39,000 years ago.
A branching green freshwater sponge forming metre-high underwater forests on Baikal's rocky slopes.
Armoured, spiny amphipods: part of a species flock of over 350 amphipods found only in Lake Baikal.
The silver fir of the European mountain forests.
The Siberian stone pine, whose nuts feed the taiga from nutcrackers to bears.
The Chinese giant salamander, up to 1.8 m, the largest living amphibian.
Tarsiers: tiny nocturnal primates with eyes each as large as their brain, and the only wholly carnivorous primates.
The Sulawesi kauri, a towering araucarian conifer tapped for dammar resin.
Heather: the low evergreen shrub that makes the moorland of Atlantic Europe, on poor, acid, often burnt ground.
Toad-headed agamas, the small lizards of Central Asian sand and gravel desert up to 5,000 m.
The timber bamboos of China, mass-flowering and dying back in cycles decades long.
The gorilla-like chalicothere of Miocene Eurasia, walking on its knuckles to keep its hooked claws sharp.
Feather grasses whose awns drill their own seed into the soil.
A hornless rhinocerotoid five metres at the shoulder and around twenty tonnes -- the largest land mammal known.
Larch -- the deciduous conifer, dropping its needles to survive the extreme continental winters of interior Siberia.
An Asian brontothere with a tall bony 'battering ram' rising from its snout, hollow and perhaps used for calling.
Palms. In the Eocene hothouse they grew at fifty degrees north beside crocodiles; their limit has been a frost line ever since.
Known from one 83 cm skull from Inner Mongolia: possibly the largest land-living carnivorous mammal, and a hoofed one.
A small Eocene browsing horse relative, found at Messel with leaves still in its stomach.
An exquisitely complete Messel primate, gut contents and all, from near the base of the primate radiation.
An Eocene oil-shale lake in Germany preserving bats, early horses and gut contents in mirror detail.
A giraffe-sized pterosaur from the Cretaceous island of Hateg in what is now Romania, apex predator of a dwarf-dinosaur fauna.
Flowering plants go from rare to dominant inside forty million years, pulling pollinating insects, fruit-eating birds and the modern structure of forests along with them.
The Asian giant tyrannosaur of the Nemegt Formation, close kin to T. rex and nearly as large.
Known for fifty years only from its 2.4 m arms; the rest turned out to be a hump-backed, duck-billed giant ornithomimosaur.
Turkey-sized and feathered, from the Gobi -- one specimen locked in combat with a Protoceratops, both buried by a collapsing dune.
The Gobi ceratopsian found with nests and eggs, and probably the origin of the griffin legend.
The largest ornithischian known: a flat-headed duck-bill fifteen metres long from Shandong.
The oldest gilled mushroom known, in 99-million-year-old Burmese amber and already entirely modern in form.
A parrot-beaked early ceratopsian, the most abundant dinosaur of the Jehol beds.
A large ornithopod with a thumb spike, and one of the first dinosaurs recognised as such.
An early beaked bird known from thousands of specimens, many with long ornamental tail streamers.
A badger-sized Jehol mammal found with a juvenile dinosaur in its stomach -- Mesozoic mammals were not all prey.
The Yixian and Jiufotang beds of Liaoning: volcanic ash falls that buried a whole forest ecosystem intact, feathers, stomach contents, colour-bearing melanosomes and all.
An aquatic Jehol plant that is among the earliest fossils confidently identified as a flowering plant.
taxa.hb: aquatic herb

taxa.note: The first dinosaur found with unambiguous filamentous feathers, and later with its ginger-and-white banded tail decoded.
A nine-metre early tyrannosauroid covered in long filament feathers -- the largest feathered animal known.
A fish-eating theropod from the English Wealden with a crocodile snout and a thirty-centimetre thumb claw; fish scales were found in its stomach.
A Chinese sauropod with a neck half its total length -- among the longest necks any animal has had.
The ginkgo lineage at its widest, in mid-latitude forests on nearly every continent. One species, Ginkgo biloba, is still alive.
A small short-tailed pterosaur from Solnhofen, and the first pterosaur ever described.
The Solnhofen 'first bird', a feathered dinosaur on a Bavarian lagoon at Laurasia's Tethyan edge.
taxa.hb: arboreal or short-flight glider

taxa.note: A long-tailed pterosaur of the same lagoons, some specimens preserving the wing membrane and throat pouch.
A dwarf sauropod six metres long, shrunk by life on the islands of the Jurassic European archipelago.
The apex predator of Jurassic Sichuan, ten metres long, hunting Mamenchisaurus and the local stegosaurs.
An early crested tyrannosauroid from the Jurassic of Xinjiang, small and long-armed, 90 million years before T. rex.
A beaver-tailed, swimming mammaliaform with preserved fur -- evidence Jurassic mammals were not all generic shrews.
A gliding mammaliaform with a preserved membrane, roughly 100 million years before bats.
One of the earliest stegosaurs, from Middle Jurassic Sichuan, still with teeth at the front of its jaws.
The first dinosaur ever formally named, from Oxfordshire, decades before anyone had the concept of a dinosaur.
An early large sauropod, originally mistaken for a giant marine reptile.
The whip-tailed sauropods -- Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Supersaurus: twenty-five metres and more of neck and tail on a comparatively light body.
Crocodile-shaped amphibians, from newt-sized to five metres, that ruled rivers and swamps for 200 million years before crocodiles took the job.
A large Triassic and Jurassic horsetail, successor to the Calamites of the Carboniferous swamps.
Mid-sized early sauropodomorphs of Early Jurassic Gondwana and beyond; nests of Massospondylus eggs show the young hatched toothless and helpless.
An early armoured dinosaur, at the base of the lineage leading to stegosaurs and ankylosaurs.
The common early sauropodomorph of Yunnan, six to nine metres long; embryos in its eggs preserve some of the oldest known organic remains in a dinosaur.
A shrew-sized nocturnal insectivore with a mammalian jaw joint -- close to the origin of mammals.
Slender, hollow-boned early theropods two or three metres long: the first widespread predatory dinosaurs.
Conifers spreading through the dry Triassic interior: the first forests built by plants that could survive a real dry season.
Long-necked, bipedal plant-eaters up to ten metres: the first dinosaurs to grow large, found in herds in Late Triassic Europe.
Armoured, pig-snouted herbivorous archosaurs common in northern Triassic red beds; extinct at the end-Triassic mass extinction.
An early long-necked sauropodomorph, and among the first genuinely large herbivorous dinosaurs.
An early pterosaur with a complex tooth battery, already fully capable of powered flight.
A reptile whose neck is longer than the rest of it combined, with only twelve vertebrae in it.
Crocodile-shaped archosaurs lurking in Late Triassic rivers before crocodiles proper existed.
A flat-skulled giant amphibian that packed drying Late Triassic lakes across Europe by the hundreds, the type genus for the metoposaurid family.
Plant-eating cynodonts with broad grinding cheek teeth -- the commonest herbivores of many Gondwanan Triassic faunas.
A pike-shaped ray-finned fish with a long toothed snout, an ambush predator of Triassic seas and lakes worldwide.
A conifer of Triassic river plains, part of the flora that recolonised the land after the end-Permian coal gap.
Flat-headed giant amphibians that mass-died in drying Triassic lakes across Laurasia.
A horsetail with paired leaves fused into sheaths, common through the Permian and Triassic of Gondwana.
Beaked, tusked herbivorous therapsids that become the most abundant large land animals on Earth.
A long-necked, semi-aquatic fish-catcher representing an early stage of the sauropterygian move into the sea.
The ammonite that dates the German Muschelkalk so precisely its zones are named after it.
Weasel- to wolf-sized therapsid predators. Unlike the gorgonopsians they got through the end-Permian extinction and hunted the Early Triassic.
A metre-tall unbranched lycopod that stands in for an entire vanished forest flora.
taxa.hb: unbranched, in disturbed coastal ground

taxa.note: A pig-sized dicynodont that survives the extinction and then makes up most of the land vertebrate fauna of the entire planet.
taxa.hb: burrowing herbivore

taxa.note: An early archosaur, sprawling and crocodile-like, at the root of the lineage that will produce dinosaurs and birds.
A worldwide fungal spike of filaments and spores at the extinction horizon itself, usually read as the rot of a collapsing land flora, though some workers argue the fossils are algae.
Kangaroos radiate as grasslands spread across the drying interior.
The platypus: egg-laying, venomous, and hunting with its eyes shut by sensing the electric fields of its prey.
The koala, living on eucalypt leaves too poor and too toxic for almost anything else.
Queen Alexandra's birdwing, the largest butterfly, with a wingspan of 28 cm.
Mulga, the wattle whose upswept leaves funnel rain to its own trunk; it covers a fifth of the continent.
A three-tonne wombat relative, the largest marsupial ever, gone from Australia around 46,000 years ago.
The marsupial lion, a powerful ambush predator with the strongest bite of any known mammal for its size.
A short-faced giant kangaroo browsing shrubs on one-toed feet.
A seven-metre monitor lizard, Australia's largest terrestrial predator until the megafauna extinction.
Early marsupial 'lions' with bolt-cutter premolars appear in the Miocene rainforest fauna.
Mihirungs or 'thunder birds': flightless giant fowl to 600 kg, relatives of ducks rather than emus.
Wombat-like browsers that reached rhinoceros size -- the largest marsupials ever.
The Chinchilla Local Fauna of the Darling Downs, Queensland -- a Pliocene assemblage recording Australia's rainforest-to-woodland shift, misfiled by name-collision with the South American rodent.
Spinifex: needle-leaved hummock grasses covering a quarter of Australia, and shelter for most of its desert reptiles.
The thorny devil: an ant-eating lizard whose skin channels dew to its mouth.
Koalas, once several genera in Miocene rainforest; one species remains, specialised on eucalypt leaves.
Banksias of the kwongan heath, one of the world's richest floras on the poorest soil.
A sheep-sized tree-dwelling marsupial herbivore, mass-preserved in Riversleigh cave pools.
A Riversleigh platypus that, unlike the living one, kept functional teeth as an adult.
Horned tortoises with clubbed tails: a Gondwanan family that survived on Lord Howe Island and Vanuatu until people reached them.
Australasia's own crocodiles, some of them land-going and some reaching Fiji and New Caledonia; the last died out after people arrived.
The grasses. Present from the Late Cretaceous, and ecologically almost invisible until about 40 Ma, when open grassland begins.
The emperor penguin, the only bird that breeds through the Antarctic winter.
A flightless midge, the largest wholly terrestrial animal on the continent.
The entire Antarctic land fauna above the microscopic -- a few dozen species surviving in moss and under stones.
The southern elephant seal, bulls of four tonnes hauling out on subantarctic beaches to fight and breed.
Antarctic hairgrass, one of just two flowering plants on the continent.
Antarctic pearlwort, one of only two flowering plants native to Antarctica.
A green alga that thrives on the guano-soaked ground of penguin rookeries, the most conspicuous plant life on the Antarctic coast.
True seals, which arose in the North Atlantic and reached the Antarctic pack ice by the late Miocene.
Penguins, flightless divers since the Paleocene; several Eocene and Oligocene species stood as tall as a person.
A bushy beard lichen, among the largest land organisms of the Antarctic Peninsula.
Mosses. They are most of Antarctica's land vegetation today, and beds of them lie freeze-dried in its Miocene tundra deposits.
Weevils of southern South America whose fossils lie in the Meyer Desert beds, 500 km from the Pole: tundra insects that outlasted the first ice sheets.
Southern conifers -- podocarps, rimu, totara -- that clothed warm-temperate Gondwana and still dominate many southern and tropical-mountain forests.
Rhino-sized South American natives with tusks and probably a short trunk -- nothing to do with elephants or tapirs, only convergent on them.
Cyperaceae: grass-like plants of wet ground, marsh and tundra, where true grasses do less well.
A fungus farming algae or cyanobacteria inside itself. Among the first things to colonise bare rock, and still the pioneer on newly exposed ground.
A small marsupial from Seymour Island: proof that mammals crossed from South America to Australia through a forested Antarctica.
Endemic hoofed mammals, some convergent on horses and camels, unique to South America.
Ants. Rare in Cretaceous amber, then from the Eocene on the dominant small predators and soil-movers of nearly every land habitat.
A small ornithopod of the high-latitude Cretaceous forests of the Antarctic Peninsula.
An Antarctic fossil placing modern bird lineages -- specifically waterfowl relatives -- before the extinction.
The first ankylosaur from Antarctica, from the James Ross Basin of the still-forested Cretaceous continent.
Giant toothless pterosaurs with stiff necks as long as a giraffe's, stalking prey on the ground like storks.
The last and largest sauropods, wide-hipped and often armoured. They are the big herbivores of every southern continent until the end of the Cretaceous.
The 'opposite birds': toothed, clawed-winged fliers that were the commonest birds of the Cretaceous and left no descendants.
Monkey-puzzle and kauri relatives: worldwide in the Mesozoic, southern-hemisphere survivors today.
The flying reptiles: wings of skin stretched on one enormously long finger, from sparrow-sized to the span of a small aircraft.
The big beaked plant-eaters with grinding tooth batteries, from Camptosaurus to the duck-bills -- the commonest large herbivores of the Cretaceous.
The Asian elephant lineage, which arose in Africa about five million years ago and spread across southern Asia.
The Indian peafowl.
The Indian rhinoceros, armour-plated in folds, of the tall-grass floodplains below the Himalaya.
The nilgai or blue bull, the largest Asian antelope.
Dipterocarps, which dominate South-East Asian rainforest to a degree no family manages anywhere else, and mast-fruit across whole regions at once.
Red oat grass or kangaroo grass, the fire-adapted dominant of savannas from Africa to Australia.
The coconut palm, spread by its own floating seeds to every tropical shore.
A large proboscidean with tusks set so close together that the trunk hung to one side; its dwarfed island forms reached Flores and Timor.
The banyan, a strangler fig that spreads on aerial roots until one tree is a grove.
Tough, mat-forming sedges whose turf makes the vast alpine meadows of high Asia and the Arctic.
Salt-excreting shrubs holding the fringes of oases and wadis.
Lemur-like early primates that spread through the greenhouse forests of the Eocene right up to the Arctic.
The 'walking whale' of Indo-Pakistani Eocene coasts, a crocodile-like stage in whale origins.
Fifty-million-year-old amber from Gujarat holds a dipterocarp rainforest, and insects with Asian relatives: India was already trading life across a narrowing sea.
A Vastan lignite mammal near the root of odd-toed ungulates, recording India's brief faunal isolation.
Termites: social cockroaches that digest wood with the microbes in their gut, and recycle most of a tropical forest's dead timber.
A horned abelisaur theropod from the Lameta beds, hunting amid the erupting Deccan Traps.
A titanosaur of latest-Cretaceous India whose nesting grounds are preserved as fossil egg clutches.
A 3.5 m snake fossilised coiled around a titanosaur egg in a nest, waiting for the hatchling.
Baleen whales reach modern size as intensified coastal upwelling concentrates their food into dense patches.
The vaquita, the smallest and rarest cetacean, confined to the turbid head of the Gulf of California.
The California sea lion, breeding on the desert islands of the Gulf of California and the Pacific coast.
The Humboldt or jumbo squid, hunting in shoals of thousands along the eastern Pacific.
Sargassum weeds, attached on warm rocky shores and, in two Atlantic species, drifting free in mid-ocean.
Flowering plants that returned to the sea in the Cretaceous, binding shallow sediment and nursing juvenile fish and turtles.
A calcified green alga that breaks down into carbonate sand -- much of a tropical beach is dead Halimeda.
Coralline red algae, crusts as hard as the rock they grow on, cementing reef rubble into reef; on a modern reef they hold more of the framework together than the corals do.
Microscopic plated algae that take over the open ocean and start building chalk.
The totoaba, a two-metre drum found only in the Gulf of California, spawning at the Colorado River's mouth.
The coelacanth, a living lobe-finned fish, survives in deep refugia off the Comoros.
The living Nautilus, a survivor of the once-vast shelled-cephalopod dynasties, still haunts these depths.
The giant squid, reaching twelve metres and known for most of history only from carcasses and sperm-whale scars.
A macropredatory shark perhaps sixteen metres long, known almost entirely from its teeth.
taxa.hb: pelagic macropredator

taxa.note: A marine ground sloth that grazed seagrass off the Peruvian coast -- a lineage no one predicted.
An early pinniped, at the transition of carnivorans into fully marine life.

Dasyclad green algae, single cells the size of a finger with whorls of branches, calcified enough to be rock-formers in Palaeozoic and Mesozoic shelf limestones; a few, like the mermaid's wineglass, survive.
The megatooth sharks, a lineage of giant whale-hunting predators running from the Eocene to Otodus megalodon.
Manta and devil rays, filter-feeders that leap clear of the water in schools of thousands.
Tunas: warm-blooded, ocean-crossing predators built for sustained speed.
Flying fishes, gliding tens of metres on enlarged fins to escape tuna and dolphinfish.
The early whales, from four-legged waders to the fully marine, serpent-bodied Basilosaurus of warm Eocene seas.
Single-celled algae in glass shells. From the Oligocene on their blooms feed the cold oceans and their remains pile up as diatomite.
Bone-eating worms that bore into whale skeletons on the sea floor; their traces go back to plesiosaur bones.
Krill: swarming shrimp-like crustaceans. In the Southern Ocean they are the single link between diatoms and everything larger -- whales, seals, penguins and fish all feed on them.
Sixgill sharks, a lineage little changed since the Jurassic, cruising the dark continental slopes.
Hard-shelled sea turtles: green, hawksbill, loggerhead and their Cretaceous forerunners.
Big flat clams littering Cretaceous seafloors, sometimes shells over a metre across.
Coiled cephalopods diversifying fast; they will become the single best index fossil of the Mesozoic.
A hook-shaped scaphitid ammonite of the Pierre Shale and the Maastrichtian chalk, one of the very last ammonites before the impact.
A rudist bivalve grown into a tall cone with a lid, packed upright in thickets that built the reefs of the Late Cretaceous Tethys in place of corals.
Keeled planktonic foraminifera raining onto the Cretaceous ocean floor.
A metre-long sea turtle of the Niobrara chalk, close to the stem of the living sea turtles.
A four-metre sea turtle, the largest ever, cruising the warm inland sea.
A slender, fast mosasaur of shallow water, the smallest of the Kansas chalk mosasaurs at two to four metres.
A plesiosaur with seventy-two neck vertebrae and a neck seven metres long, from the Kansas chalk; its first describer put the head on the tail.
A three-metre sea turtle of the Western Interior Seaway, ancestor in form to Archelon, with a shell reduced to struts.
A small pterosaur of the Kansas chalk with an antler-like crest half again as long as its skull.
A deep-bodied plethodid fish of the Niobrara sea with a fan-like dorsal fin the length of its back.
A shark with pavement teeth for crushing clams, ten metres long, a Cretaceous durophage whose teeth litter the chalk seas of two hemispheres.
Large conical foraminifera of Cretaceous carbonate platforms, big enough to see without a lens.
A thick, coiled oyster with a spiral beak, cemented to the Cretaceous sea floor in beds you can walk on in Texas and Alabama.
The 'Ginsu shark', seven metres long, whose bite marks are on the bones of mosasaurs and plesiosaurs from Kansas to Europe.
A slit-shelled sea snail of Jurassic and Cretaceous shelves; its relatives survive today only in deep water.
The smallest and most numerous photosynthesiser known, making a large share of the oxygen produced by the open ocean.
Tiny vase-shaped plankton that zone the Tethyan latest-Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.
A calcified red alga growing in nodules and crusts on Ordovician to Cretaceous reefs; sliced, its pink and grey banding is the 'beetroot stone' of Jurassic England.
Tangled tubes of a calcified cyanobacterium, coating shells and grains into oncoids on Cambrian to Jurassic sea floors: the commonest microbial fossil of the Palaeozoic shelf.
The largest ray-finned fish that has ever lived, sixteen metres of filter-feeder from the Oxford Clay, straining the Jurassic sea like a whale shark.
A crocodile rebuilt for the open sea: flippers, a tail fin, no armour, hunting fish and ammonites in the Oxford Clay.
Whales and dolphins: hoofed mammals that returned to the sea in the Eocene and became its largest predators and filter-feeders.
The sooty tern, which stays on the wing for years at sea and breeds in vast colonies on tropical islets.
The Portuguese man o' war, a colony of specialised animals sailing under a gas-filled float.
Free-floating sargassum, the golden weed of the Sargasso Sea, carrying its own community of fish, crabs and turtles.
Turtle grass, forming the great seagrass meadows of the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico.
Pyrosomes: glowing colonial tunicates, hollow tubes that can grow longer than a whale.
Giant marine lizards, relatives of monitors and snakes, that took the top-predator role in every Late Cretaceous sea.
A Late Cretaceous belemnite whose bullet-shaped guards fill the Maastricht chalk; its oxygen isotopes were among the first used to read past sea temperatures.
They displace corals as the main tropical reef builder for much of the Cretaceous, and die at the K-Pg.
A thick, ornamented triangular clam that burrowed Jurassic and Cretaceous sands worldwide; a lone survivor, Neotrigonia, still lives off Australia.
A horseshoe crab preserved at the end of its own death-track across the anoxic mud.
An ichthyosaur with eyes the size of dinner plates, the largest of any vertebrate relative to its body, for hunting squid in the dark.
A long-necked plesiosaur of the Oxford Clay with a hundred needle teeth, netting small fish and squid.
A short-necked pliosaur with a skull well over a metre long, hunting other marine reptiles.
taxa.hb: pelagic pursuit predator

taxa.note: Stone corals appear from nowhere and rebuild the reef ecosystem the Permian destroyed; every modern reef descends from them.
The dugong, the one strictly marine sea cow left, grazing seagrass from the Red Sea to the Coral Sea.
A small seagrass of the Red Sea and western Indian Ocean, growing from the shallows to fifty metres down.
Giant kelp; kelp forests establish as a new nearshore biome in newly cool coastal waters.
The seagrass of Saya de Malha, a drowned bank in mid-ocean carrying the largest seagrass meadow on Earth.
'Sea sawdust', a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium whose rust-coloured blooms streak warm, nutrient-poor seas.
The wandering albatross, with the widest wingspan of any living bird, circling the Southern Ocean between breeding seasons.
Star-shaped calcareous nannoplankton whose extinction near 1.9 million years ago is used to close out the warm Pliocene ocean.
Sperm whales in their Miocene variety, from dwarf forms to Livyatan, a raptorial hunter of other whales.
Large brown algae forming underwater forests on cool rocky coasts. A Neogene novelty, and the habitat sea otters and abalone depend on.
Planktic foraminifera colonise the open water column, becoming a permanent part of the ocean's carbon cycle.
The 'saber-toothed herring', a fanged predatory fish found in Late Cretaceous seas world-wide.
Squid-like cephalopods whose bullet-shaped guards are among the commonest Jurassic fossils.
A late ammonite that grew shells a metre across, among the last of its kind, in the seas of the final Cretaceous stages worldwide.
The crow shark, a scavenger of the Cretaceous seas whose serrated teeth are found lodged in dinosaur bones washed out to sea.
A planktonic foraminifer with a double keel, the zone fossil of the Late Cretaceous ocean; the K-Pg boundary clay is full of its broken shells.
Layered mounds built by microbial mats trapping and binding sediment: the dominant reef of the first three billion years, and often the only fossil a Precambrian shelf preserves.
The sperm whale, the largest toothed predator alive, diving past two kilometres to hunt squid in the dark.
Clams, mussels, oysters and scallops. They take over the shallow sea floor from brachiopods after the end-Permian and never give it back.
The bowhead whale, adapted to break sea ice, is the signature large animal of the modern Arctic.
Polar cod: it lives in and under the sea ice and is the link between Arctic plankton and everything larger.
The narwhal, whose spiral tusk is a single tooth carrying millions of nerve endings.
Larger benthic forams diversify and become key shelf-carbonate contributors.
The Greenland shark, the longest-lived vertebrate known; individuals are thought to reach four centuries.
Oceanic dolphins, from spinners to orcas; a late-Miocene radiation that now fills every sea.
Grenadiers or rattails, the commonest fishes of the continental slope and the abyssal plain.
After the Messinian salinity crisis dried the basin, salt-tolerant survivors and Atlantic recolonisers rebuild the fauna.
The leatherback, a half-tonne turtle that follows jellyfish from the tropics to subpolar water.
The great white shark, descended from broad-toothed makos about six million years ago.
Neptune grass: a flowering plant whose meadows anchor the Mediterranean's endemic shelf ecosystem; single clones are thought to be tens of thousands of years old.
Eelgrass, the seagrass of cool northern shores, nursery to cod, scallops and brent geese.
Coin-sized benthic foraminifera beginning the bank-building that will define Tethyan shelf carbonates.
taxa.hb: benthic on warm carbonate shelves

taxa.note: An endemic brackish-water mussel that swarmed the isolated, freshening Paratethyan basins.
Lanternfishes, perhaps the most abundant vertebrates on Earth, rising hundreds of metres to the surface every night.
The snow leopard, hunting blue sheep across cliff and scree.
The Himalayan griffon, soaring the highest of any vulture.
The bharal, the snow leopard's principal prey.
The kiang, the wild ass of the Tibetan Plateau.
Sal, the dipterocarp that forms the forests of the Himalayan foothills and central India.
Mammoths spread across the newly cold northern continents as the mammoth steppe forms.
Beavers. Most fossil ones were burrowers, not dam-builders; the Ice Age giant beaver was the size of a black bear.
Deer, the antlered ruminants of the northern forests. They reached South America with the interchange and never got south of the Sahara.
A 'shovel-tusker': a gomphothere whose lower jaw ends in a broad pair of flat tusks, used for stripping bark and cutting plants.
Royal ferns, a genus so conservative that a Jurassic rhizome from Sweden is cell for cell like a living one.
The Andean condor, riding ridge updraughts on a three-metre wingspan.
The vicuna, grazing the altiplano on the finest wool of any mammal.
Aquatic water frogs breathing through skin folds in cold high-altitude lakes.
The queen of the Andes: a bromeliad that grows for eighty years at 4,000 m, flowers once on a ten-metre spike, and dies.
The South American giant short-faced bear: early arrivals after the interchange may have stood three metres tall and weighed over a tonne.
An armoured, car-sized relative of armadillos, native to South America -- the interchange traveller into North America was its relative Glyptotherium.
The tropical giant ground sloth, as big as Megatherium, ranging from Brazil through Panama to Florida.
A bizarre caiman with a long, flat, duck-like snout, probably a filter-feeder straining small prey from the water.
Over 250 species of small lizards from Patagonia to the high Andes -- one of the largest lizard radiations anywhere.
Cypresses, junipers, redwoods and their kin; their fossil wood lies in the Miocene lavas of Kerguelen, now a treeless island.
The bald eagle, a fish eagle of North American lakes, rivers and coasts.
Lodgepole pine, whose cones open only in fire.
Totora, the giant bulrush of Lake Titicaca from which the Uros build boats and floating islands.
The American pika, haying all summer on talus slopes and retreating uphill as the mountains warm.
The North American beaver, whose dams engineered the continent's stream valleys.
White-tailed and mule deer, the New World's own deer and its commonest large mammals.
The coast redwood, the tallest tree on Earth, in the fog belt.
Camels are a North American family. They crossed to Asia about 7 Ma and to South America about 3 Ma, then died out where they began.
Horses: fifty million years of North American evolution, from four-toed forest browsers to one-toed grazers, exported to the Old World in pulses and then lost at home.
The Alpine ibex, grazing near-vertical rock.
The Alpine marmot, hibernating eight months of the year.
The Eurasian lynx, ambush hunter of roe deer in forest and mountain.
The capercaillie, the turkey-sized grouse of old conifer forest.
The European larch, a deciduous conifer at the timberline.
The moose: the largest deer, browsing willow and feeding in boreal lakes, its splayed hooves suited to bog and snow.
The Barbary macaque of the Atlas cedar forests, the only monkey north of the Sahara; in the Pleistocene it ranged to England.
Tapirs have barely changed since the Eocene. Today's odd range -- tropical America and Malaya -- is what is left of a family once spread across the north.
The Barbary sheep or aoudad of the Saharan massifs and the Atlas.
The bearded vulture or lammergeier, which lives on bones and drops them on rocks to break them.
The wild boar, ploughing forest floors from Portugal to Japan.
A Chadian skull around seven million years old, close to the chimpanzee-human split and arguably on our side of it.
The Late Jurassic Morrison Formation - Allosaurus, Stegosaurus, Apatosaurus, Diplodocus - the archetypal dinosaur bonebed.
A small feathered paravian preserved well enough for its actual colour pattern to be reconstructed from melanosomes.
A crested early theropod, six metres long and nothing like its film portrayal.
The conifer whose logs make the Petrified Forest, transported and buried in seasonal river systems.
A slender early theropod dinosaur, hundreds found together at Ghost Ranch in Pangaea's western deserts.
taxa.hb: gracile bipedal predator, gregarious

taxa.note: Heavy-bodied browser
taxa.hb: heavy-bodied browser

taxa.note: A slender, long-snouted phytosaur from the Late Triassic of the eastern United States, crocodile-like in build though unrelated, with nostrils set back near the eyes rather than the snout tip.
The last of the giant temnospondyls, five metres long, surviving in the cold rift-valley rivers of polar Australia where crocodiles could not live.
A short-necked sauropod with two rows of tall spines down its neck, perhaps carrying a sail or a display of horn.
The Late Jurassic Tanzanian beds preserve Giraffatitan and Kentrosaurus - Africa's answer to the Morrison.
Australia's Jurassic sauropod, about fifteen metres long -- one of very few windows on the continent's Jurassic land life.
An early sauropodomorph from Mount Kirkpatrick, 4,000 m up in the Transantarctic Mountains.
One of the earliest true sauropods, from Zimbabwe, as Gondwana begins to break apart.
A crested theropod from the Transantarctic Mountains, showing dinosaurs living at high southern latitudes.
An early sauropodomorph from South African Jurassic red beds, known even from embryos in the egg.
A turkey-sized early ornithischian from the Karoo with three kinds of teeth, including tusks, in one jaw.
The forked-leaf seed fern that defines Gondwanan Triassic forest and marks the end of the coal gap.
taxa.hb: forked-frond tree and shrub

taxa.note: The seed-bearing organ of Dicroidium, the seed fern that dominated Triassic Gondwana.
A heavy ten-metre sauropodomorph of Late Triassic Argentina, already walking on all fours.
A boar-sized traversodont cynodont, the commonest herbivore of Ischigualasto -- and found in India too, across an unbroken Gondwana.
One of the earliest dinosaurs of all: a three- to six-metre predator from Ischigualasto, when dinosaurs were still a minor part of the fauna.
A metre-long, light-boned dinosaur from the dawn of the group, with teeth suited to both meat and plants.
A seven-metre rauisuchian, the apex predator of Ischigualasto while the first dinosaurs ran about its feet.
A dog-sized cynodont with differentiated teeth and probably fur -- most of the way to a mammal.
taxa.hb: terrestrial predator

taxa.note: Squat, spiny-cheeked parareptiles a hand or two long. They crossed the end-Permian extinction and were everywhere in the Triassic.
An abundant tusked herbivore whose disappearance defines the terrestrial extinction horizon in the Karoo.
A bear-sized gorgonopsian with sabre teeth, the apex predator of the last Permian ecosystems.
taxa.hb: terrestrial apex predator with sabre canines

taxa.note: The earliest well-known cynodont, from the Late Permian of the Karoo, Zambia and Germany, with a paddle-like tail that suggests it swam.
A tongue-leaved seed fern blanketing Gondwana, whose distribution across five now-separate continents was early evidence for continental drift.
taxa.hb: woody tree in very wet soils, like a modern bald cypress; conical, widely spaced crowns to exploit low-angle polar light

taxa.note: The segmented root of the Glossopteris trees, preserved in Antarctic peat and Indian coal: the plumbing of a forest that grew in polar light.
taxa.hb: septate, air-filled roots in waterlogged soil

taxa.note: A strap-leaved cordaitalean of the Glossopteris flora, growing beside the seed ferns in the cool-temperate forests of Permian Gondwana.
Tree-sized horsetails forming dense stands along channel margins.
taxa.hb: clonal thickets on levees and channel margins

taxa.note: A sabre-toothed predator of the Late Permian Karoo, top of the food chain before the Great Dying.
A boomerang-headed amphibian of Permian ponds, its skull drawn out into broad lateral horns.
A thick-skulled, barrel-chested dinocephalian of the Karoo: a three-metre herbivore built for head-butting.
The commonest large animal of the middle Permian Karoo, a two-and-a-half-metre pareiasaur with a warty hide, in herds on the floodplain.
A pig-sized dicynodont that dug spiral burrows in the Karoo floodplain; the most abundant vertebrate fossil of the Late Permian of South Africa.
A freshwater shark with an eel's body and a long spine at the back of the head, hunting the coal-swamp rivers and lakes for a hundred million years.
Stocky lizard-shaped early reptiles, some with several rows of teeth for grinding plants -- among the first small herbivores on land.
Massive, thick-skulled therapsids, likely head-butting, that go extinct at the end of the interval.
As glossopteris but with non-midribbed leaves
taxa.hb: as Glossopteris but with non-midribbed leaves

taxa.note: A small aquatic reptile of Permian Gondwanan lakes, found on matching shores in Brazil and South Africa - Wegener's evidence for drift.
A eurypterid of the Permian of Brazil, one of the last of its kind, in the rivers and lakes of Gondwana.
A cold-climate seed plant of the floras that recolonised bare ground as the Karoo ice sheets melted.
Cold marine faunas in the seas around a Gondwana buried under Carboniferous ice.
A small tree lycopsid of Carboniferous Argentina, growing in the outwash plains in front of Gondwana's glaciers.
The seed fern that marks the Permian red beds across Euramerica: the flora of a continent that had lost its swamps.
An early conifer in drier upland settings -- the beginning of forest that is not a swamp.
Giant predatory lobe-finned fish of the Carboniferous rivers of Laurussia.
Seed ferns with enormous fronds and the largest seeds of the Palaeozoic.
A fern-like seed plant of Carboniferous Gondwana, the commonest fossil of the cold country between the ice sheets; its name is a flora as much as a plant.
A fern-like seed plant with fan-shaped leaflets, the signature plant of the Early Carboniferous of eastern Australia and Argentina.
A thirty-metre lycopsid that grew fast, reproduced once and toppled -- the principal ingredient of coal.
taxa.hb: unbranched pole with a crown, DETERMINATE growth - grew, reproduced once, died

taxa.note: An early horsetail of the Mississippian wetlands, ancestral to the giant Calamites that would build the coal swamps.
A slender sphenopsid with wedge-shaped leaves in whorls, a scrambling plant of Carboniferous and Permian swamps on every continent.
Stoneworts: green algae of clear fresh water that stand like tiny horsetails and coat themselves in lime; their oospores are the commonest plant fossil of ancient lake beds.
A small placoderm with a tall crest on its trunk armour, in fresh water from Greenland to Antarctica and Australia: the first fish genus shown to span both hemispheres.
The first plant with a woody trunk and a true leafy canopy -- effectively the first modern-looking tree.
taxa.hb: the first true forest tree: real wood, roots to ~1 m, a spreading crown

taxa.note: Early sparse vegetation of horsetails and progymnosperms on the southern floodplains.
A Late Devonian tetrapod known from a jaw found in New South Wales, the first sign that the earliest four-limbed animals were in Gondwana as well as in Greenland.
An antiarch placoderm so abundant and widespread it is effectively the index fossil of Devonian fresh water.
A brachiopod that marks the Devonian seas of the Americas, from the Appalachian basin to the cool southern shelves.
The Gilboa tree: a trunk topped by a frond crown, and the oldest known forest stand.
taxa.hb: palm-like crown of frond-like branches

taxa.note: A Middle Devonian clubmoss with hooked leaf tips for climbing, known from New York to Australia: one of the first plants to spread across both hemispheres.
The oldest fossil of a land organism with cord-forming mycelium. Fungi were rotting and binding the first soils before there were plant roots to put in them.
The Bokkeveld Group and Parana Basin preserve the cold-water Devonian brachiopod-trilobite province.
The Petoskey stone: a colonial rugose coral of Devonian reefs whose six-sided corallites turn up as pebbles on Lake Michigan beaches.
Sessile on carbonate shelves
taxa.hb: sessile on carbonate shelves

taxa.note: Green algae established in shallow water; the ancestors of every land plant are somewhere in this group.
Red algae persist through the glaciations in shallow refugia.
The Middle Devonian fishes of the Aztec Siltstone in the Transantarctic Mountains -- placoderms, acanthodians, lungfish and early sharks in rivers and lakes at 30 degrees south.
A sprawling Devonian lycopsid with sickle-shaped leaves, among the first plants with true leaves, on the shores of Laurussia and China alike.
A few centimetres of leafless forking stem with a spore capsule on top: the first vascular plant, and the ancestor of every forest.
taxa.hb: tiny dichotomising axes in damp lowlands

taxa.note: A lycophyte with real leaves, appearing surprisingly early in Australia and complicating every tidy story about plant evolution.
taxa.hb: creeping and upright shoots with true microphylls

taxa.note: Ringed, tapering shells a centimetre long, in such numbers that they pave Devonian bedding planes; what the animal was is still argued.
A Devonian plant known from spore capsules on short stalks, close to the mosses; found in Belgium, China and Australia.
A giant eurypterid with grasping claws, one of the largest arthropods that ever lived.
taxa.hb: nektonic sea scorpion with crushing chelicerae

taxa.note: Diagnostic of the cold high-latitude Gondwanan realm.
taxa.hb: benthic, cold-water shelf

taxa.note: Bony fishes, which split early into ray-fins and lobe-fins; one branch of the lobe-fins leads to everything with four limbs.
Millipede-grade arthropods, among the first animals to live permanently out of water.
An index brachiopod of the cool Silurian Malvinokaffric seas, unlike anything in the tropics.
A distinctive low-diversity cold-water shelly province across South America, South Africa and the Falklands.
The 'Dudley bug', a trilobite so abundant in the Silurian limestone of the English Midlands that the town put it on its coat of arms.
Liverwort-grade plants -- the first land vegetation, known from cryptospores rather than bodies.
Vase-shaped microfossils -- testate amoebae that built shells and, by implication, had something to hide from.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, found inside the earliest land plants. Those plants had no roots, so the fungus was the root; the partnership still runs about eighty percent of plant species today.
Biological soil crust binding sand between rains, the desert's living skin.
Single-row graptolites that swarm Silurian seas, evolving so fast that they date the rocks they drift into.
Robust, strongly enrolling trilobites that dominate the cold high-latitude Ordovician shelves where reefs are absent.
A 'sun coral', a tabulate whose tubes stand in a honeycomb of finer ones, building Silurian and Devonian reefs with Favosites and Halysites.
The straight-shelled nautiloid of the Baltic 'Orthoceras limestone', a metre-long swimmer whose chambered shells pave the floors of Swedish churches.
A single-stemmed graptolite with square-cut cups, the drifting plankton of Late Ordovician black shales on every continent.

Tillite: the unsorted rubble a glacier leaves, cemented to rock. Gondwana's Carboniferous-Permian tillites lie on five continents, and their scratched pavements were among the first evidence that those continents had once been one.
The enrolled trilobite of the Cincinnati hills, found curled into a ball by the thousand; the commonest trilobite of Late Ordovician North America.
A cold-water brachiopod assemblage that spread worldwide as end-Ordovician ice gripped the Saharan pole.
A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, metres long, hunting the Ordovician carbonate platform.
Heat- and sulphur-loving microbes at the base of food webs run entirely on chemistry, not light.
A calymenid trilobite of the cold, muddy shelves that ringed high-latitude Gondwana.
A jawless armoured fish of Ordovician Gondwana, tadpole-shaped with a bony head shield, in shoals along the Bolivian shore.
Single-celled prokaryotes with no nucleus, forming the mats and stromatolites that dominate the fossil record for most of Earth's history.
The tuning-fork graptolite, two branches hanging from a float; a colonial drifter whose fossils zone the Early Ordovician worldwide.
Moroccan mudstones extend Burgess-type soft-bodied preservation into the Ordovician of the Saharan shelf.
Large, smooth-shelled trilobites, some with eyes on stalks, that dominate many Ordovician carbonate platforms.
The zigzag burrow that defines the base of the Cambrian: an animal probing the sediment from below, worldwide, at a level no body fossil can match.
Colonial corals with honeycomb skeletons, joining stromatoporoids as reef builders.
The earliest articulate brachiopods, ribbed and nearly symmetrical, abundant on Ordovician shelves.
A burrowing brachiopod that survives everything and looks much the same today.
Colonial hemichordates drifting in open water, whose fast turnover makes them the timekeepers of the Ordovician.
Small conical Cambrian shells with a lid and a pair of props. What they actually were was argued for 175 years -- probably relatives of brachiopods.
A tiny blind agnostid trilobite that drifted worldwide, which is what makes it the middle Cambrian's best time-marker.
The defining Cambrian arthropod: armoured, mobile, with compound eyes made of calcite crystals.
A large spiny trilobite of the Baltic-Avalonian 'Atlantic' province, unknown on Cambrian Laurentia.
A bag-shaped animal armoured with star-shaped spicules, sessile on Cambrian sea floors, whose isolated stars are among the commonest small shelly fossils.
A metre-long swimming predator with grasping appendages, and the first animal large enough to sit at the top of a food web.
taxa.hb: active nektonic swimmer with lateral flaps

taxa.note: A lobopodian whose net-patterned armour plates were known as small shelly fossils for decades before the Chengjiang animal that wore them turned up.
A large, spiny redlichiid trilobite that typifies the Cambrian shelves of Gondwana and China.
taxa.hb: benthic

taxa.note: A cup-shaped reef builder of the early Cambrian, sponge-grade animals that made the first animal reefs and were gone by the middle of the period.
A South Australian Lagerstatte where Anomalocaris keeps its compound eyes - tens of thousands of lenses each.
Sponge-grade cone-shaped reef builders that made the first animal reef framework and were extinct within twenty million years.
An early Cambrian trilobite of the West Gondwanan shelves, and the marker of the Bigotinid province.
A tiny coiled shell of the earliest Cambrian, snail-like or a mollusc's cousin, found from Siberia to Newfoundland and marking the base of the Tommotian.
A three-lobed tube a few millimetres long, among the first mineralised skeletons of the Cambrian and a zone fossil of its opening stage on every continent.
Glass sponges building a reef belt along the Tethyan shelf larger than any reef system before or since.
Shelled filter feeders that will dominate the shelf benthos for the next three hundred million years.
Sponges. Molecular clocks and disputed biomarkers place their origin in the Tonian or Cryogenian; unambiguous body fossils come later.
Partly buried, sack-like, in shifting sand
taxa.hb: partly buried, sack-like, in shifting sand

taxa.note: Stacked calcareous cones that built the first animal reefs, and carry the first drill holes made by a predator.
taxa.hb: gregarious tube-dweller, reef-forming

taxa.note: A goblet-shaped skeletal organism from the Nama Group, part of the first mineralised reef community.
taxa.hb: stalked, attached to microbial reefs

taxa.note: A fractal frondose Ediacaran of the Namibian shelf, type of the whole rangeomorph group.
Sheaths of a filamentous cyanobacterium, the mat-builder of Proterozoic tidal flats, preserved in chert on every craton.
A segmented Ediacaran form with a shield-like head end, argued over for decades as a possible early arthropod relative.
A flat, segmented, centimetre-to-metre oval that left feeding traces as it moved; cholesterol in its tissues shows it was an animal.
taxa.dt: external digestion of the mat beneath it
taxa.hb: flat on a microbial mat, possibly mobile

taxa.note: A quilted, vane-like Ediacaran organism of the terminal-Ediacaran Nama sandflats.
Frond-shaped rangeomorphs anchored to the sea floor, feeding without a mouth or a gut.
taxa.hb: sessile frond anchored by a holdfast, in the deep sea below the photic zone

taxa.note: A bilaterally symmetrical grazer that scraped mats with a feeding structure -- the best candidate for an early mollusc relative.
taxa.hb: mobile bottom-dweller

taxa.note: Spiny organic-walled microfossils that make the Doushantuo a global Ediacaran reference.
A colonial coccoid cyanobacterium of Proterozoic cherts, all but identical to the living Entophysalis of tropical tidal flats.
Sheets of carbonate laid straight on top of glacial debris as a snowball Earth ended, under an atmosphere carrying hundreds of times today's CO2.
Alternating iron-rich and silica-rich layers precipitated from a ferruginous ocean. They largely stop forming by 1.85 Ga, once the deep sea holds oxygen.
The heart urchin of the English chalk, whose changing shape up through the cliffs was one of the first fossil lineages read as evolution.
A flightless, toothed diving bird that swam the seaway like a loon.
taxa.hb: flightless foot-propelled diver, toothed

taxa.note: A mid-sized mosasaur, the commonest in the Kansas chalk, preserved with skin, a forked tail fin and the contents of its gut.
A stalkless crinoid that drifted in colonies of hundreds and sank together, leaving slabs of the Kansas chalk covered in its arms.
A seven-metre pliosaur of the Early Jurassic, with nostrils built to smell under water, from the same Yorkshire and Somerset shales as Dactylioceras.
Streamlined, live-bearing marine reptiles; Mary Anning's Lyme Regis specimens are how the world learned they existed.
Long-necked, four-flippered marine reptiles rowing through shallow Jurassic seas.
Thick heart-shaped bivalves crowding the Triassic Tethyan carbonate platforms.
Eel-like chordates known mostly from their tooth elements, which become the finest stratigraphic tool in the Palaeozoic.
The 'Rhaetic bone bed' bivalve, small and asymmetric, crowding the last sea floors of the Triassic in Europe.
A thin-shelled bivalve that drifted or lay in shoals over the whole Late Triassic ocean; its beds date Norian rocks from Alaska to New Zealand.
A thin flat 'paper clam' blanketing deep Tethyan Triassic seafloors along the drifting blocks.
A globular Carnian ammonoid, the zone fossil of the late Carnian on both sides of Pangaea.
A knobbly ceratitid ammonoid of the Carnian, in the Alps and the Tethys; its extinction near the Carnian Pluvial Episode.
A flat, paper-thin bivalve of Triassic deep-shelf muds, often found in mass-mortality pavements.
A small long-necked marine reptile found by the thousand in Guizhou Triassic shales.
One of the earliest ichthyosaurs: within a few million years of the extinction, reptiles are already back in the sea.
Meadows of stalked crinoids ('sea lilies') whose disarticulated ossicles make crinoidal limestone.
A thin-shelled bivalve that carpets post-extinction seafloors -- the classic disaster taxon.
The ammonoid whose first appearance defines the base of the Triassic.
Leaf-like calcareous algae that grew in thickets on Pennsylvanian and Permian sea floors and built mounds hundreds of metres across -- the reef builders of an age with few corals.
Rice-grain foraminifera, abundant and fast-evolving enough to date the Carboniferous limestones they largely consist of.
A rugose coral of Permian Tethyan reefs, colonial and thickly walled.
A Late Permian ammonoid with complex sutures on the road to the ammonites proper, from the Tethyan reefs of Timor.
A spiny productid brachiopod that anchored itself in soft mud with hair-fine spines, a Permian shell of cool and warm seas alike.
Ammonoids with frilled-saddle sutures, radiating from a handful of end-Permian survivors to become the standard timekeepers of the Triassic.
A thin-shelled bivalve that paves the black, oxygen-poor shales of Jurassic Europe -- the 'Posidonia Shale' -- by the million.
Silica-shelled plankton whose ooze hardens into the deep-sea cherts that record vanished ocean floors.
A giant ichthyosaur reaching twenty metres, comparable to a modern large whale.
taxa.hb: pelagic

taxa.note: An early ichthyosaur up to seventeen metres long with an eel-like body and no dorsal fin, from Nevada's Middle Triassic sea.
Palaeozoic ammonoids with zigzag sutures, abundant in the open water above Devonian to Permian shelves and basins.
A scallop-like bivalve of the late Palaeozoic, in every shelf sea from the Mississippian to the end of the Permian.
A small solitary horn coral of Pennsylvanian and Permian shelves, standing alone in the mud between the brachiopod beds.
A winged, strongly ribbed spiriferid brachiopod, common enough in the Permian to have been used as a guide fossil across Pangaea's shelves.
A crinoid with a twisted stem and a low cup, from the Mississippian crinoid gardens of Indiana and Iowa where sea lilies grew in meadows.
A bryozoan built as a corkscrew: a lacy fan wound round a spiral axis, named for the screw, and a rock-former in Mississippian limestones.
A blastoid: a bud-shaped echinoderm on a stalk, with five feeding grooves, so abundant in the Mississippian of the Mississippi valley that they are sold by the jar.
The 'scissor-tooth shark', with a single blade of teeth in each jaw that never shed; a Pennsylvanian predator the size of a great white.
A mosasaur over twelve metres long, the apex predator of the seaway that split North America.
A ferocious bony fish, sometimes fossilised with an entire swallowed fish inside it.
A straight-shelled ammonite so abundant it zones the entire seaway; the chalk records its coccolith plankton.
A barrel-shaped rudist, one of the strange bivalves that grew in thickets and built the reefs of the Late Cretaceous tropics in place of corals.
Dinoflagellates: armoured plankton whose resting cysts are the sea's fine-grained clock, and whose symbionts make a reef coral's colour and food.
A small clam so abundant and fast-evolving it dates the whole boreal Jurassic-Cretaceous.
taxa.hb: cool-water shelf, gregarious

taxa.note: A large, late ichthyosaur found world-wide in Early Cretaceous seas; some Australian specimens are preserved as opal.
A giant short-necked pliosaur, apex predator of the cold Cretaceous sea over central Australia.
The grey wolf, once the most widely distributed wild land mammal on Earth.
A spike-shouldered aetosaur from the Late Triassic American Southwest, armoured along back and flanks and rooting through the soil with a pig-like snout.
Sabre-toothed therapsid predators with an erect gait -- the first mammal-line animals that hunt like mammals.
A Late Permian reptiliomorph of the Angaran wetlands, close to the ancestry of amniotes.
A horsetail relative with whorls of broad leaves, characteristic of the Cathaysian flora.
A dicynodont of the Junggar Basin at the very end of the Permian, one of the tusked plant-eaters that were about to inherit the Earth.
Strap-leaved coniferophytes up to thirty metres tall on the drier ground beyond the mires: the first vegetation that would read as forest rather than swamp.
taxa.hb: tree with strap-shaped leaves; coastal and upland

taxa.note: A Cathaysian seed plant with broad net-veined leaves that look startlingly like an angiosperm's, 150 million years early.
taxa.hb: climbing or scrambling, with large net-veined leaves

taxa.note: A pareiasaur of the Late Permian of Shanxi, a barrel-bodied plant-eater armoured with bony studs.
The pareiasaur of Kotelnich, known from dozens of skeletons, a plant-eater the size of a cow.
A small anomodont from Kotelnich with a grasping hand and long tail: the earliest tree-climbing vertebrate known.
A heavily built pareiasaur from the Russian Permian, knobbly-skulled and barrel-bodied.
Barrel-bodied synapsids with absurdly small heads: Cotylorhynchus reached four metres and was the first really large plant-eater on land.
A bull-sized Russian dinocephalian carrying horn-like bosses on its skull -- a signature Angaran animal.
A Chinese dinocephalian therapsid: the Cathaysian block's own big Middle Permian predator, on a landmass separated from the rest.
Extinct beaked insects with a third pair of winglets, sucking on Carboniferous plant reproductive organs.
A small early reptile with chewing teeth, of the Permian of Texas and, as its relative Belebey, of Russia and China.
Tall, usually unbranched, in coal swamps
taxa.hb: tall, usually unbranched, in coal swamps

taxa.note: A sail-backed synapsid predator, more closely related to us than to any dinosaur, and routinely mis-sold as one.
taxa.hb: terrestrial apex predator with a tall neural-spine sail

taxa.note: The largest land animal of its day: a caseid with a body like a barrel and a head that looks borrowed from something a tenth its size.
An early sail-backed synapsid, and one of the first large herbivorous land vertebrates.
A heavy-bodied temnospondyl amphibian, effectively the crocodile of Permian rivers.
A two-metre millipede, the largest land arthropod that has ever existed, leaving trackways across swamp floors.
taxa.hb: ground-dwelling

taxa.note: A dragonfly relative with a wingspan approaching three-quarters of a metre, possible only in a high-oxygen atmosphere.
taxa.hb: aerial predator, ~70 cm wingspan

taxa.note: Produced the largest pollen grains known.
taxa.hb: scrambling or self-supporting, with very large fronds

taxa.note: Long-bodied, eel-like reptiliomorphs of the coal-swamp pools -- fish-eating ambush predators close to the ancestry of amniotes.
One of the first true reptiles, sheltering in hollow lycophyte stumps in Nova Scotia.
taxa.hb: insectivore living in hollow lycopsid stumps

taxa.note: A seven-metre freshwater lobe-finned predator, the largest freshwater fish known.
An Angaran seed fern, its fronds among the commonest plant fossils of the Kuznetsk Basin coal measures.
A 70 cm scorpion of the Scottish coal-age forests, with compound eyes and book lungs -- a land hunter, not a swimmer.
A small, slender East Kirkton tetrapod, close to the origin of fully terrestrial amniotes.
Stalked crinoids that rafted on driftwood over the open sea.
The ammonoid group that radiated through the Triassic from the handful of lineages that survived the end-Permian bottleneck.
Straight-shelled cephalopods whose conchs pave the Baltic orthoceratite limestone -- the rock takes its name from them.
A planispiral snail-like mollusc, coiled in one plane like a tiny nautilus, grazing Carboniferous and Permian sea floors.
A smooth, rounded brachiopod, the single most abundant shell of Carboniferous and Permian limestones in North America.
Solitary and colonial Palaeozoic corals, extinguished entirely; the corals that follow are a different lineage.
The goniatite that names its group: a globular ammonoid with zigzag sutures, a swimmer of Mississippian seas on every continent.
A spiriferide brachiopod that spread almost worldwide in the Late Devonian, as the earlier provincial faunas merged.
A wrinkled, flat-lying brachiopod with a sharp bend at the edge, one of the longest-lived shell genera of the Palaeozoic.
Colonial, honeycomb corallites
taxa.hb: colonial, honeycomb corallites

taxa.note: A round, finely ribbed brachiopod with a spiral feeding organ inside, in nearly every Silurian and Devonian shelf sea in the world.
A Late Devonian goniatite whose disappearance marks the Frasnian-Famennian extinction, one of the five great ones.
A Middle Devonian index fossil of the Old World Realm.
taxa.hb: benthic, attached

taxa.note: A long-lived conodont whose cone-shaped elements are in almost every Ordovician and Silurian limestone; the animal itself was a small eel-like swimmer.
Sea scorpions, in decline for a hundred million years, finally gone.
A ray-finned fish of the Kupferschiefer copper-shale, preserved as the sea first flooded then stagnated.
Spiny, thick-shelled brachiopods resting on soft carbonate mud, the dominant shellfish of the late Paleozoic sea floor.
A sphinctozoan sponge, a string of beads with a canal through them, one of the builders of the Permian Reef of Texas.
Pig-sized reptiles with a parrot beak and shearing tooth plates. In places they are half of all the fossils found -- then gone by the Norian.
The characteristic Angaran leaf - cool temperate, seasonal, deciduous.
taxa.hb: deciduous tree with strong growth rings

taxa.note: A tree fern whose trunk was a mantle of adventitious roots rather than wood. It took over the mires as the giant lycopsids faltered.
taxa.hb: tree fern with a mantle of adventitious roots

taxa.note: The Late Permian tetrapods of Kotelnich on the Vyatka: pareiasaurs, gorgonopsians and the earliest cynodont-like therapsids, from a riverbank where they are found standing in their burrows.
Scale trees beginning their takeover of coastal mires -- the coal machine is warming up.
A tetrapod so close to the amphibian-amniote boundary that its placement has flipped repeatedly.
Spider-like arachnids among the first land predators -- there was already something worth hunting.
The wolverine: a mustelid that kills prey many times its size and caches it in the frozen ground.
Siberian spruce, the taiga's dominant tree across the range.
Mountain avens, the tundra mat-plant whose leaves in lake mud named the Younger Dryas cold snap.
The tiger, from Siberian taiga to Sumatran rainforest.
A two-metre sprinter from the Isle of Wight -- the small, fast plant-eater of the Wealden floodplain.
Crocodile-line archosaurs that walked upright on pillar legs: the top land predators of the Triassic, before dinosaurs had the role.
The big tusked dicynodonts of the Triassic -- ox-sized, beaked herbivores found on every part of Pangaea.
The Permian coal flora of the Kuznetsk Basin: Rufloria and Cordaites forests with Angaropteridium beneath them, the counterpart in cool Angara of the Glossopteris forests of the south.
A gymnosperm of the Angaran flora, from a Permian Siberia too cold for the coal swamps of the tropics.
The American black bear, the range's largest surviving carnivore.
A tyrannosauroid of Appalachia, the eastern island of Cretaceous North America, with long arms its western cousins had lost.
Dragonflies, damselflies and their giant Palaeozoic cousins the griffinflies: aerial predators for 325 million years.
One of the earliest seed plants; the seed is what eventually lets vegetation leave the water's edge.
taxa.hb: small woody plant

taxa.note: A large predatory lobe-fin hunting in the same rivers as the first tetrapods, and eating them.

Tapering trunks up to eight metres tall standing over a landscape where nothing else reached the knee. Carbon isotopes point to a fungus rather than a plant, making it the largest organism on land for 40 million years.
taxa.hb: free-standing column, the tallest organism of its day

taxa.note: A Devonian relative of Arthropleura, an early millipede-grade detritivore of the first forest floors.
A lobe-finned fish with the limb bone arrangement of a tetrapod already inside its fin.
The tree of the Gilboa 'forest' in New York - the oldest known forest, of fern-like Wattieza trees.
An early arachnid that made silk from spigots set in plates rather than spinnerets: silk long before webs.
One of the earliest ray-finned fishes, a fast predator of the Devonian lakes of Scotland and Quebec, ancestral in form to half the vertebrates alive.
An early lycopsid of the Devonian of China and Europe, low and branching, before the tree forms of its group.
The Devonian trilobite of New York and Ohio, once called Phacops rana, whose eye lenses were read for the evolution of vision.
A winged spiriferide brachiopod of the Middle Devonian Appalachian seas, its hinge drawn out into long points.
A half-metre arthrodire of the Old Red Sandstone lakes and seas of Scotland, armoured over the head and trunk and naked behind.
A cladoxylopsid tree from the oldest forest floors known. It shed whole branches rather than leaves, and its roots began cracking rock into soil and drawing CO2 out of the air.
The trilobite with the compound eyes of stacked calcite lenses, each one visible to the naked eye; a Devonian reef-dweller found enrolled by the hundred.
A bony-shielded jawless fish of Old Red Sandstone rivers and lakes.
A trilobite with a long tail spine and large crescent eyes, a swimmer or fast crawler of the Silurian shelf.
Sea scorpions patrolling brackish lagoons, some large enough to take vertebrate prey.
Chain coral, a diagnostic Silurian reef builder whose colonies form linked palisades.
taxa.hb: colonial reef builder, chain-like

taxa.note: A solitary horn coral, the simplest of the rugose corals, standing on its tip in the Ordovician mud.
A large Silurian brachiopod that formed dense shell banks across carbonate shelves.
A wide, flat strophomenid brachiopod that lay on the mud like a dropped coin, the most abundant shell in the Ordovician limestones of the American Midwest.
One of the largest trilobites.
taxa.hb: benthic burrower

taxa.note: A branching bryozoan whose colonies are dotted with star-shaped mounds; in the Cincinnatian it is a rock-forming fossil.
An edrioasteroid, a disc of an echinoderm that cemented itself to shells and fed with five curved arms; a group with no living relatives.
A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, possibly six metres long, hunting the shelf seas.
taxa.hb: nektonic, with a long straight conical shell

taxa.note: One of the oldest vertebrates with a skeleton, a jawless fish clad in mosaic bony plates, from the Ordovician of Colorado.
An early tetrapod with eight fingers and internal gills -- limbs evolved in the water, not for walking on land.
A more robust tetrapod from East Greenland, able to haul itself but still tied to water.
taxa.hb: amphibious, with limbs but a fish-like tail

taxa.note: A flat-headed predator with a neck, wrists and lungs, found in Arctic Canada exactly where and when the rocks predicted it would be.
Jawed fish encased in articulated bony armour; for sixty million years they run the seas, then vanish completely.
An early vascular plant carrying sporangia along the sides of its stems, on the line that leads to the lycophytes.
An early lycophyte with leaf-like enations along a branching stem, and rooting structures that are not yet true roots.
A springtail from the Rhynie chert, ~410 Ma: the oldest known hexapod, and effectively a modern-looking one.
Rhynie chert jaws of disputed affinity, argued to be the oldest insect -- possibly even a winged one.
From the Rhynie chert, and the earliest clear evidence of arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis - land plants have always been partly fungal.
taxa.hb: rootless, in a hot-spring wetland

taxa.note: A Scottish hot-spring deposit that silicified an entire Early Devonian land ecosystem where it stood.
A millipede from ~425 Ma Scotland with open spiracles -- the oldest direct evidence of an animal breathing air.
A stubby Silurian millipede of the earliest land litter, feeding on decaying plant matter beside water.
Colonial encrusters and branching forms that build much of the reef and hardground framework.
A blind trilobite with three long spines, sometimes fossilised walking in single-file 'conga lines' across the sea floor.
A tiny, blind agnostid trilobite, a few millimetres long and so widespread that it zones Cambrian rocks across several continents.
The late Cambrian trilobite of the Baltic alum shales, living in black oxygen-poor mud that preserved it in its thousands.
The trilobite everyone has held: Elrathia kingii from Utah's Wheeler Shale, quarried by the million from a low-oxygen shelf it had almost to itself.
A scale-covered mat grazer whose affinities have been argued between molluscs and annelids for a century.
taxa.hb: benthic, armoured with sclerites and spines

taxa.note: The commonest animal of the Burgess Shale, a thumbnail-sized arthropod with sweeping head spines; thousands of specimens, no close living relative.
A burrowing priapulid worm, the commonest predator of the Burgess Shale sea floor, found with hyoliths in its gut.
A lancelet-like swimmer from the Burgess Shale with a notochord and V-shaped muscles: one of the oldest chordates.
The 508-Ma community of British Columbia - the fullest window on Cambrian soft-bodied animals anywhere.
A spiny olenellid trilobite that defines the Laurentian faunal province of the Cambrian tropics.
taxa.hb: benthic

taxa.note: A spined, stilt-legged lobopodian reconstructed upside-down and backwards for decades before anyone got it right.
taxa.hb: benthic walker

taxa.note: Fractal, self-similar fronds anchored in deep water at Mistaken Point -- a body plan with no modern counterpart.
Shows evidence of reproduction by stolons.
taxa.hb: reclining on the sea floor, deep water

taxa.note: A bush-shaped rangeomorph, its fronds radiating from a common base rather than standing on a stalk.
Organic-walled cysts of algae, too poorly understood to classify but abundant enough to date rocks with.
Calcified sponges that are the principal reef framework builders of the Middle Palaeozoic.
Silurian Gotland is a fossilised barrier reef of tabulate and rugose corals and stromatoporoids.
The lace-collar trilobite: blind, with a pitted fringe around the head that filtered the mud it ploughed through.
A large asaphid trilobite of the Baltic Ordovician, some species carrying their eyes on long stalks to see over soft mud.
The red 'Orthoceras limestone' of Sweden and Estonia is a graveyard of straight-shelled cephalopods.
A big asaphid trilobite of the Baltoscandian Ordovician, common in the orthoceratite limestones.
Colonial corals built from stacked tubes with floors across them. Palaeozoic reef framework, extinct at the end-Permian.
Alum-shale nodules of Sweden preserve millimetre crustaceans in uncrushed three-dimensional phosphate.
An olenellid trilobite of the early Cambrian Baltic and Laurentian shelves.
A large olenellid trilobite of the early Cambrian Scandinavian shelf.
One of the oldest trilobites of Baltica, from the earliest Cambrian shelly faunas.
The omul, the whitefish on which Lake Baikal's fishery has always rested.
The Siberian crane, breeding on Arctic wetlands and wintering five thousand kilometres south.
Dahurian larch, the only tree that forms forest on continuous permafrost.
Golomyanka: translucent, scaleless Baikal fish, a third oil by weight, bearing live young in open water.
Reindeer lichen, the tundra's dominant winter forage.
Bears. Omnivorous, wide-ranging, and one of the few large carnivores that hibernates through a boreal winter.
Cottongrass, whitening Arctic bogs in summer and building the tussocks of the tundra.
Woolly fringe-moss, the grey carpet over the lava fields of Iceland and Jan Mayen.
Bears: big omnivorous carnivorans of the northern continents, reaching South America with the interchange, where the spectacled bear is the last of the giant short-faced line.
Rhinoceroses were once the commonest large herbivores of the northern continents, with hornless, hippo-like and woolly forms; five species remain.
The last forests before the Great Dying, buried under the largest volcanic eruption of the eon -- the coal seams of Tunguska are their remains.
Amphibians and early reptiles of the Permian rivers, the northern counterparts of the Karoo fauna.
A horsetail with unbranched stems, the Angaran and Gondwanan counterpart of Calamites, along every Permian riverbank of Siberia and the Glossopteris country.
Scorpions: among the first arachnids ashore, and scarcely changed in outline since the Carboniferous.
Jawless armoured fish, bottom-feeding and slow, and the only vertebrates in the water.
Wood-producing plants that still reproduce by spores -- the structural revolution before the reproductive one.
